lessons.title: Bridge grammar: relative clauses
lessons.bigQuestion: How do relative clauses add information without starting a new sentence?
objectives: To use relative clauses beginning with who, which, where, when, whose or that
successCriteria: All: identify the relative clause and its relative pronoun
Most: write relative clauses with commas to add extra information
Some: choose the right relative pronoun for people, things, places and times
lessons.smsc: Cultural: the achievements of ancient civilisations

keywords.def: a clause that adds information about a noun, starting with who, which, where, when, whose or that
the word that starts a relative clause
placed inside another sentence
a naming word

hook.text: The Great Pyramid was built for Khufu. It is near Cairo. It took about 20 years to build. Can you make this one sentence without losing any facts?
hook.a: For example: The Great Pyramid, which is near Cairo, was built for Khufu over about 20 years.

resources: Bridge week 1: Year 5 grammar essential (missed Autumn: Pharaohs, Scream Machine)
Punctuation Intervention Booklet (Lesson 6: Brackets, dashes, hyphens and ellipses) for pupils who need extra support
Mini-whiteboard and pen
Exercise book

starter.q: Join with because: The Nile flooded. Farmers could grow crops.
starter.a: Farmers could grow crops because the Nile flooded.
A group of words with a verb

starter.q: Give a noun from ancient Egypt

head: Pronoun
Used for
Example
rows: the pyramid, which is made of stone,
in summer, when the Nile flooded,
the king, whose tomb was hidden,

model.problem: The Nile is the longest river in Africa. It flows north.
steps: Main clause: The Nile flows north.
Extra information: it is the longest river in Africa
Relative pronoun for a thing: which
Embed with commas: The Nile, which is the longest river in Africa, flows north.
model.answer: The Nile, which is the longest river in Africa, flows north.

teach.heading: Common error
teach.note: who is for people, which is for things.

misconception.wrong: The scribe, which wrote on papyrus, was clever.
misconception.right: The scribe, who wrote on papyrus, was clever.

check.q: Giza, ___ the pyramids stand, is near Cairo.
check.why: Giza is a place, so where. who is for people; which would need "in which".

practice.q: Underline the relative clause: The cat, which was sacred, slept in the temple.
practice.a: which was sacred
practice.model: Teacher works this one aloud: read the question, underline the key words, link it to today's rule, then give the answer in a full sentence: which was sacred

practice.q: Add a relative clause: The pharaoh ___ was buried in a tomb.
practice.a: For example: The pharaoh, who ruled for 30 years, was buried in a tomb.

practice.q: Choose: The boy ___ father was a scribe learned to write. (who / whose)
practice.a: whose

independent.q: Core: combine six pairs of sentences about ancient Egypt using relative clauses (in the portal response box, with the sentence starter and paragraph frame)
independent.a: For example: Papyrus, which grew by the Nile, was used to make paper.
independent.model: Teacher does the first part aloud before pupils start, showing each step: For example: Papyrus, which grew by the Nile, was used to make paper.

independent.q: Extend: write four sentences of your own, each with a different relative pronoun
independent.a: Sentences using who, which, where, when

independent.q: Stretch: write a sentence with a relative clause that has no commas because it is essential information
independent.a: For example: The tomb that Carter found in 1922 belonged to Tutankhamun.

exit.q: Which relative pronoun is used for places?
Add commas: The Sphinx which has a lion's body guards the pyramids.
exit.a: The Sphinx, which has a lion's body, guards the pyramids.

lessons.homework: Write five sentences about your home or school using a different relative pronoun in each. Read for 20 minutes a day.
lessons.send: SEND: relative pronoun cards with picture cues (person, thing, place, time). EAL: model sentence frames. Stretch: use a relative clause after a preposition (the river in which...).

lessons.title: Bridge grammar: modal verbs and adverbs of possibility
lessons.bigQuestion: How do writers show how certain or uncertain something is?
objectives: To use modal verbs and adverbs to show degrees of possibility
successCriteria: All: identify modal verbs in sentences
Most: order modal verbs and adverbs from certain to uncertain
Some: choose modals and adverbs precisely for predictions and persuasion
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: Muslims say in sha Allah (إِنْ شَاءَ اللَّه) about the future, because only Allah knows it for certain

islamicLink.text: Muslims say in sha Allah (إِنْ شَاءَ اللَّه) about the future, because only Allah knows it for certain

keywords.def: a verb that shows how likely something is, like might, should, will
how likely something is
an adverb like perhaps, certainly, probably
a guess about the future based on evidence

hook.text: It will rain tomorrow. It might rain tomorrow. It must rain tomorrow. Which is the most certain? Can anyone be completely certain about tomorrow?
hook.a: "will" and "must" sound certain; "might" is uncertain. Only Allah knows the future for certain, so Muslims say in sha Allah.

pictures.find: metal spoon in hot water photograph

resources: Display: modal verbs scale
Vocabulary Intervention Programme (Lesson 5: Shades of meaning) for pupils who need extra support
Mini-whiteboard and pen
Exercise book
Bridge week 2: Year 5 grammar essential

starter.q: Add a relative clause: The star ___ is very bright.
starter.a: For example: The star, which is called Sirius, is very bright.
A guess about the future based on evidence

teach.heading: Adverbs of possibility
teach.note: Combine with modals: The comet will probably appear at dawn.

model.problem: Predict what happens to a metal spoon in hot water.
steps: Evidence: metals are good thermal conductors
Certainty: high, so will
Adverb: almost certainly
Sentence: The spoon will almost certainly feel hot within a minute.

check.q: Which sentence is most certain?
check.why: will plus definitely shows the highest certainty.

practice.q: Underline the modal verb: You should wear a coat.
practice.a: should
practice.model: Teacher works this one aloud: read the question, underline the key words, link it to today's rule, then give the answer in a full sentence: should

practice.q: Make it less certain: The bus will be late.
practice.a: For example: The bus might be late.

practice.q: Add an adverb of possibility: The star ___ formed billions of years ago.
practice.a: For example: probably

independent.q: Core: rewrite six sentences to show a different level of certainty (in the portal response box, with the sentence starter and paragraph frame)
independent.a: For example: It will snow. → It might possibly snow.
independent.model: Labelled model to go through first (Predict what happens to a metal spoon in hot water.): Evidence: metals are good thermal conductors | Certainty: high, so will | Adverb: almost certainly | Sentence: The spoon will almost certainly feel hot within a minute. | Result: A precise prediction.

independent.q: Extend: write four predictions for a science test with modals and adverbs
independent.a: For example: The ice will probably melt within ten minutes.

independent.q: Stretch: explain why a scientist might write "may" instead of "will"
independent.a: Because results are not certain until tested

exit.q: Which phrase do Muslims say about the future?

lessons.homework: Write five sentences about plans for the weekend using different modal verbs (and in sha Allah where it fits). Read for 20 minutes a day.
lessons.send: SEND: modal verb cards to place on the scale. EAL: visuals for certain and uncertain. Stretch: use modals for persuasion (You must try...).

lessons.title: Bridge grammar: parenthesis with brackets, dashes and commas
lessons.bigQuestion: How can I add extra information to a sentence without confusing the reader?
objectives: To use brackets, dashes and commas to add parenthesis
successCriteria: All: identify parenthesis in a sentence
Most: add parenthesis using brackets, dashes or commas
Some: check the sentence still makes sense when the parenthesis is removed
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: the Qur'an tells us that Allah placed the stars to guide people through the darkness of land and sea (6:97)

islamicLink.text: The Qur'an tells us that Allah placed the stars to guide people through the darkness of land and sea (6:97)

keywords.def: extra information added to a sentence, which could be removed
the marks ( ) around extra information
a short line used in pairs around extra information
a mark that can also be used in pairs for parenthesis

hook.text: Sentence: Jupiter is the largest planet. Add one extra fact in the middle without starting a new sentence. How would you show it is extra?
hook.a: For example: Jupiter (the fifth planet from the Sun) is the largest planet.

resources: Punctuation Intervention Booklet (Lesson 6: Brackets, dashes, hyphens and ellipses) for pupils who need extra support
Display: punctuation posters
Mini-whiteboard and pen
Exercise book
Bridge week 2: Year 5 grammar essential

starter.q: Add a relative clause: Mars ___ is red.
starter.a: For example: Mars, which is called the Red Planet, is red.

teach.heading: Three ways
teach.note: All work in pairs around the extra information.

head: Mark
Example
rows: Saturn (famous for its rings) is a gas giant.
Saturn - famous for its rings - is a gas giant.
Saturn, famous for its rings, is a gas giant.

model.problem: The Moon (which has no air) orbits the Earth.
steps: Find the extra information: which has no air
Remove it
Read: The Moon orbits the Earth.
Still makes sense, so the parenthesis is correct

teach.heading: Pairs, not singles
teach.note: The second mark is often forgotten.

misconception.wrong: Venus, the hottest planet is covered in cloud.
misconception.right: Venus, the hottest planet, is covered in cloud.

check.q: Which uses parenthesis correctly?
options: The Sun (a star is very hot.
The Sun (a star) is very hot.
The Sun a star) is very hot.
check.why: Brackets must open and close around the extra information.

practice.q: Add brackets: Mercury the smallest planet is closest to the Sun.
practice.a: Mercury (the smallest planet) is closest to the Sun.
practice.model: Teacher works this one aloud: read the question, underline the key words, link it to today's rule, then give the answer in a full sentence: Mercury (the smallest planet) is closest to the Sun.

practice.q: Add dashes: The telescope a gift from my uncle is in the garden.
practice.a: The telescope - a gift from my uncle - is in the garden.

practice.q: Add commas: Neptune the farthest planet is very cold.
practice.a: Neptune, the farthest planet, is very cold.

independent.q: Core: add parenthesis to six sentences about space using all three methods (in the portal response box, with the sentence starter and paragraph frame)
independent.model: Teacher does the first part aloud before pupils start, showing each step: Six correct sentences

independent.q: Extend: write four sentences of your own about the night sky with parenthesis
Stretch: explain when brackets might be better than commas
independent.a: For example: brackets for extra facts like dates, so they stand out clearly

exit.q: Add commas: Saturn the ringed planet is huge.
exit.a: Saturn, the ringed planet, is huge.
Remove the parenthesis: the sentence must still make sense

lessons.homework: Find two examples of parenthesis in a newspaper or book and copy them. Read for 20 minutes a day.
lessons.send: SEND: sentence strips to cut and insert the extra information. EAL: model sentences. Stretch: use a relative clause as parenthesis inside dashes.

lessons.title: Grammar: cohesion within and between paragraphs
lessons.bigQuestion: How do I make my report flow so each paragraph links to the next?
objectives: To build cohesion with adverbials, pronouns, synonyms and topic sentences
successCriteria: All: use adverbials to link sentences
Most: vary references to a noun with pronouns and synonyms
Some: link paragraphs with topic sentences that refer back
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: properties and changes of materials
lessons.smsc: Social: writing that is easy for others to follow

keywords.def: how ideas link together across a text
a word or phrase that links ideas, like however or this metal
a word or phrase that tells how, when or where, or links ideas
a word with a similar meaning

hook.text: Read: "Iron is strong. Iron is magnetic. Iron rusts. Copper conducts electricity." Why does this feel choppy? How could we fix it?
hook.a: Use pronouns, synonyms and linking adverbials: Iron is strong and magnetic; however, this metal rusts...

resources: Display: TiPToP paragraphing posters
Cohesive devices word mat
Mini-whiteboard and pen
Pupil's report plan

starter.q: Synonym for metal (in a report on iron)
starter.a: For example: this element, the material
The first sentence of a paragraph saying what it is about

model.problem: Iron is strong. Iron is magnetic. Iron rusts.
steps: Combine: Iron is strong and magnetic.
Contrast adverbial: However,
Synonym instead of repeating: this metal
Result: Iron is strong and magnetic. However, this metal rusts when it is exposed to water and air.

teach.heading: Linking paragraphs
bullets: End one paragraph with a hint
Start the next by referring back
teach.note: Show two paragraphs joined by a referring-back topic sentence.

check.q: Best start for a paragraph on copper after one on iron?
options: Unlike iron, copper does not rust easily.
check.why: B refers back to iron and introduces copper: cohesion between paragraphs.

practice.q: Replace the repetition: Gold is soft. Gold does not tarnish.
practice.a: Gold is soft. This precious metal does not tarnish.
practice.model: Teacher works this one aloud: read the question, underline the key words, link it to today's rule, then give the answer in a full sentence: Gold is soft. This precious metal does not tarnish.

practice.q: Link with an adverbial: Aluminium is light. It is strong.
practice.a: For example: Aluminium is light. Furthermore, it is strong.

independent.q: Core: rewrite a choppy 8-sentence paragraph using three types of cohesive device (in the portal response box, with the sentence starter and paragraph frame)
independent.model: Labelled model to go through first (Iron is strong. Iron is magnetic. Iron rusts.): Combine: Iron is strong and magnetic. | Contrast adverbial: However, | Synonym instead of repeating: this metal | Result: Iron is strong and magnetic. However, this metal rusts when it is exposed to water and air. | Result: A cohesive paragraph.

independent.q: Extend: write two linked topic sentences for your report sections
Stretch: highlight every cohesive device in your rewrite and name its type

exit.q: Give one cohesive device for contrast

lessons.homework: Underline the linking words in a page of your reading book. Read for 20 minutes a day.
lessons.send: SEND: device word mat; rewrite four sentences. EAL: synonyms list for metal words. Stretch: use ellipsis (missing out repeated words) for cohesion.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Poetry - The Eagle and writing about nature
lessons.title: Reading The Eagle
objectives: Read a poem aloud with expression
Explain what a poem is about using evidence

keywords.def: a group of lines in a poem
a steep rough rock
bright blue
a flash of lightning with a crash of thunder

starter: Bismillah. Add a linking adverbial: ___, the sun set.
Correct the tense: She runs and fell.
Add parenthesis: The eagle a powerful bird flew.

teach.heading: Meet the poem
bullets: The Eagle by Alfred, Lord Tennyson
It describes an eagle on a cliff
teach.note: Introduce Tennyson as a famous Victorian poet. Read the poem aloud twice. He clasps the crag with crooked hands; / Close to the sun in lonely lands, / Ring'd with the azure world, he stands. / The wrinkled sea beneath him crawls; / He watches from his mountain walls, / And like a thunderbolt he falls. (Alfred, Lord Tennyson, The Eagle) Ask pupils what picture they see.

teach.heading: Understanding the words
teach.note: Use context and images. Ask how the eagle is described in the first stanza (still, high up) and in the second (hunting, falling).

teach.heading: What happens?
bullets: Stanza 1: the eagle stands high up
Stanza 2: it watches and then dives
teach.note: Ask pupils to summarise each stanza in a sentence. Highlight the change from stillness to action. Link to the final line as a dramatic climax.

teach.heading: The bird's point of view
bullets: The sea 'crawls' from the eagle's height
We see the world as the eagle does
teach.note: Ask: how does the sea look from a mountain? Why does it 'crawl'? Link to perspective. Be cautious: ask for pupils' ideas first.

teach.heading: Respond to the poem
bullets: What does the poem make you feel?
teach.note: Invite personal responses. Link to appreciating the beauty of creation. Mention that the Qur'an invites reflection on birds: Surah al-Mulk 67:19 refers to birds above us with wings spread and folded. Keep it brief and respectful.

practice: What does 'azure' mean?
In which line does the eagle attack?
How many lines are in each stanza?
independent: Read the poem aloud with a partner, one stanza each.
Answer six questions about the poem.
Draw the scene and label with words from the poem.
exit: Which word shows the eagle is strong?
What does the final line suggest?
lessons.homework: Learn the first stanza by heart.
lessons.send: SEND: highlight key words and use picture support. EAL: pre-teach crag, azure, thunderbolt. Stretch: write a short paragraph on how the poem's mood changes.

lessons.title: Figurative language for free verse: the olive tree
lessons.bigQuestion: How can a poem without rhyme still sound like a poem?
objectives: To understand how free verse uses imagery, line breaks and figurative language instead of rhyme
successCriteria: All: identify simile, metaphor and personification in a free verse poem
Most: explain the effect of one line break
Some: write three lines of free verse about the olive tree
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: plants and life cycles (the olive tree)
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: the olive is named in the Qur'an as a blessed tree

islamicLink.text: Allah swears by the fig and the olive (at-Tin 95:1), and the Qur'an describes a blessed olive tree whose oil almost glows (an-Nur 24:35). The olive is a sign of Allah's blessings.

keywords.def: poetry with no regular rhyme or rhythm
where a line ends; it can create a pause or emphasis
words that create pictures in the mind
giving human qualities to something that is not human

hook.text: An olive tree can live for over a thousand years. If it could speak, what would it remember?
hook.a: Answers vary: seasons, harvests, travellers, storms, families resting in its shade.

pictures.alt: the twisted trunk of an ancient olive tree

resources: Tarbiyyah Primary Year 5 curriculum map 2023-24, Ground-Breaking Greeks text types (no school English scheme for this project among the files) (free verse)
Teacher's model free verse poem: Old Olive (on slides; written for this lesson)
Vocabulary Intervention Programme (Lesson 15: Similes, metaphors and personification) for pupils who need extra support
Children's dictionary and thesaurus (book or online)
Mini-whiteboard and pen

starter.q: What were Olympic wreaths made from?

teach.heading: What is free verse?
teach.note: Read the teacher's model poem Old Olive aloud twice.

head: Line (from the model)
Technique
Effect
rows: its trunk is a twisted rope

teach.heading: The power of a line break

left.title: One line
points: The old tree waits for rain.

steps: Image: Silver leaves turn in the wind
Personification: as the old tree hums to itself
Line break for emphasis: and waits.
model.answer: Silver leaves turn in the wind / as the old tree hums to itself / and waits.

check.q: Which is most likely free verse?
options: Roses are red, violets are blue...
Grey stones / under a white sky / still
check.why: B has no rhyme or regular beat and uses line breaks. A and C rhyme in a fixed pattern.

practice.q: Write a metaphor for the olive trunk
practice.a: For example: The trunk is a knotted fist.
practice.model: I do: think of its shape (twisted, knotted) and compare it to something strong: The trunk is a knotted fist.

practice.q: Write a simile for olive leaves
practice.a: For example: leaves like silver fish

practice.q: Where would you break: The tree has stood here for a thousand years
practice.a: For example: The tree has stood here / for a thousand years.

independent.q: Core: write a free verse poem of six to eight lines about the olive tree, the sea or the stadium, with at least one simile, metaphor and personification
independent.model: Labelled model: Image: Under the hot hill sky, | Personification: the olive tree stretches its arms | Simile: its leaves flicker like silver fish | Metaphor: its roots are anchors in the stone. | Line break for emphasis: It stays.

independent.q: Extend: explain the effect of one line break
independent.a: For example: breaking before "It stays" makes the reader pause and feel how still the tree is

independent.q: Stretch: use one sound technique (alliteration or onomatopoeia)
independent.a: For example: the sea hisses on the shingle

exit.a: B) no regular rhyme or rhythm

lessons.homework: Find a tree near your home. Write three lines of free verse about it. Read for 20 minutes a day.
lessons.send: SEND: frame of line starters (The tree is..., Its leaves are like..., It...). EAL: word bank with pictures of olive trees. Stretch: write a second verse from the tree's point of view.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Poetry - The Eagle and writing about nature
lessons.title: Sound and structure: rhyme, alliteration and rhythm
objectives: Identify rhyme scheme, alliteration and rhythm
Perform a poem with expression

keywords.def: words that end with the same sound
words close together that begin with the same sound
the beat of the words in a poem
the pattern of rhymes in a poem

starter: Bismillah. Name the three types of figurative language.
Is 'the sea crawls' a simile or personification?
Write a metaphor about a mountain.

teach.heading: Rhyme
bullets: Each stanza has one rhyme sound
teach.note: Tap out rhymes while rereading. The rhyme scheme is AAA BBB. Ask why a triplet (three rhyming lines) might help give a feeling of power.

teach.heading: Alliteration
bullets: clasps the crag with crooked hands
teach.note: Underline the 'c' sounds in the first line and the 'w' sounds in the second stanza. Ask what the hard 'c' sounds suggest, such as grip and strength.

teach.heading: Rhythm
bullets: Count the beats in each line
The lines have a strong steady beat
teach.note: Clap the rhythm. Note that each line has four strong beats. Do not over-explain. Pupils feel the pattern. Ask whether the last line sounds quicker.

teach.heading: Perform it
bullets: Pause at semicolons and full stops
teach.note: Model a performance. Show how punctuation guides the voice. Pairs rehearse and perform. Offer feedback on clarity and expression.

teach.heading: Why sounds matter
teach.note: Draw out the idea that poets choose words for sound as well as meaning. Contrast hard sounds (c, k, t) with soft sounds (s, l, m) and invite pupils to give their own examples.

practice: Which word rhymes with 'lands'?
Find two words in the poem that begin with the same sound.
How many lines are in the poem?
independent: Label the rhyme scheme and alliteration in the poem.
Perform the poem with a partner and record two improvements.
Write four lines using alliteration about a river.
exit: Write two alliterative words for a storm.
What is the rhyme scheme of The Eagle?
lessons.homework: Write a four-line rhyming verse about a bird.
lessons.send: SEND: use coloured pens to mark rhyme and alliteration. EAL: practise reading in chunks. Stretch: write a short analysis of how sound supports meaning in the final line.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Poetry - The Eagle and writing about nature
lessons.title: Writing our own nature poem
objectives: Plan and write a short poem about an animal
Use figurative language and sound devices deliberately

keywords.def: a section of a poem
words that create pictures in the mind
first version
improve

starter: Bismillah. Name two sound devices.
Write a simile about a hawk.
What is personification?

teach.heading: Choose your subject
bullets: Choose one you can picture clearly
teach.note: Brainstorm animals and what they do. Link to the beauty of creation: observing creatures is a way to reflect on Allah's creation. Avoid attributing statements to texts that are not certain.

teach.heading: Gather words
teach.note: Model gathering vocabulary for 'The Owl' or 'The Fox'. Encourage precise verbs. Ask pupils to find unusual but accurate words.

teach.heading: A model poem
bullets: The fox slips through the silver frost,
a shadow stitched to the sleeping hedge.
teach.note: Read the model. Identify alliteration (slips... silver... sleeping), personification, metaphor ('Moonlight is his lantern'). Ask what picture the poem creates. Show how the poem uses two short stanzas.

teach.heading: Write a draft
bullets: Aim for a strong last line
teach.note: Pupils write drafts. Circulate to suggest improved verbs. Reassure pupils that their poems need not rhyme.

teach.heading: Reading and improving
bullets: Change one word to make it stronger
teach.note: Pairs share and give a star and suggestion. Ask volunteers to perform. Celebrate effort.

practice: Write three precise verbs for your animal.
Write one metaphor.
Write one phrase with alliteration.
independent: Write a poem of two stanzas about an animal.
Label the figurative language in your poem.
Write a title.
exit: What sound device did you use?
lessons.homework: Improve your poem and write a neat copy.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a word bank and frame. EAL: allow a draft in simple sentences first. Stretch: write in rhyme with a consistent scheme.

lessons.unit: Unit 3: Suspense - reading and writing a tense scene
lessons.title: Reading a suspense extract
objectives: Identify how an author builds suspense
Infer feelings from details in a text

keywords.def: a feeling of excitement or worry about what will happen
nervous strain in a story
three dots ... showing a pause or something unfinished
the mood of a setting

starter: Bismillah. Recall: name three poetry devices.
Add parenthesis: The house an old one stood still.
Write a linking adverbial for the start of a paragraph.

teach.heading: What is suspense?
bullets: The reader wants to know what happens next
The pace slows or speeds up
teach.note: Ask pupils about moments in films or books where they felt tense. Explain that suspense is created by what the author chooses to show and hide.

teach.heading: Read the extract
bullets: Light shines from a door that should be dark
teach.note: The old house was silent. Nadia crept up the stairs, her hand sliding along the cold banister. One step creaked. She froze. Somewhere above her, something shifted. A long, slow scrape ... then nothing. Her heart hammered. The door at the top of the stairs was open - just a crack - and a thin line of yellow light spilled onto the landing. She had not left a light on. Had she? Read slowly in a hushed voice.

teach.heading: Techniques
teach.note: Underline each technique. Ask pupils what each does. Short sentences increase pace; an ellipsis creates a pause; the question leaves the reader uncertain.

teach.heading: What do we infer?
teach.note: Ask how we know. Use evidence: 'Her heart hammered', 'She had not left a light on'. Model a P.E.E. answer.

teach.heading: What happens next?
teach.note: Link to modal verbs. Pupils predict: 'Nadia might find a stranger, or perhaps a cat.' Ask them to justify with clues.

practice: Find a short sentence that shows Nadia was afraid.
What does 'Her heart hammered' suggest?
What is unusual about the light?
independent: Answer six questions about the extract with evidence.
Create a table: technique, example, effect.
Write a prediction using modal verbs.
exit: Name one way the author builds suspense.
lessons.homework: Find a tense moment in a book you are reading and note the techniques.
lessons.send: SEND: highlight techniques in colour. EAL: pre-teach banister, landing, froze. Stretch: write a short paragraph on how the pace changes.

lessons.unit: Unit 3: Suspense - reading and writing a tense scene
lessons.title: Suspense techniques in writing
objectives: Use short sentences, senses and questions to create tension
Vary sentence length for effect

keywords.def: how fast or slow a story moves
a sentence with few words that creates drama
describe actions and details instead of naming feelings
a question that does not need an answer

starter: Bismillah. What is suspense?
Give one technique used in the extract.
Add an ellipsis to this: Then nothing happened.

teach.heading: Show, don't tell
bullets: Show: Her hands shook. She held her breath.
Details make readers feel the fear
teach.note: Offer a flat sentence and ask pupils to show the feeling instead. Collect actions for fear: trembling, frozen, wide eyes, pounding heart.

teach.heading: Control the pace
teach.note: Show a paragraph with a mix: a long sentence full of detail followed by a very short one. Ask what the short sentence does. Warn against overuse of short sentences.

teach.heading: Use the senses
